title: Interfaces vs abstract classes
idea: An interface names a role a class promises to play; an abstract class is a partial implementation that shares state and steps with its subclasses.

analogy.text: An interface is a job advert: anyone skilled can apply, and one person may hold several jobs. An abstract class is a franchise kit: shared kitchen, fixed recipe.
analogy.breaks: Default methods let an interface ship some behaviour too.

points: A class implements many interfaces but extends exactly one class.
Interfaces hold no instance fields; abstract classes keep state and constructors.
Depend on the interface; offer an abstract base only to share real code.
In interviews, start with an interface; add an abstract class when duplication appears.

hero.title: Clients see the role, not the base

steps.caption: `Dashboard` knows only the `Report` interface. It calls `render()` and nothing else.
`AbstractReport` implements the role once. It owns the title and the fixed layout of `render()`.
`SalesReport` extends the base and writes only `body()`. Layout code is not repeated.
`StockReport` does the same. A layout change edits one class and reaches every subclass.
`RemoteReport` skips the base and implements `Report` directly. The interface leaves that door open.
Interface for the type, abstract class for shared code. `List` and `AbstractList` in the JDK follow this shape.

code.title: Interfaces as roles
code.caption: One record plays two roles. Each caller depends only on the role it needs.

walk.text: `Priced` declares what a priced thing can do. It holds no fields, only a contract.
A default method gives shared behaviour. Implementers may keep it or override it.
A static method is a helper tied to the interface, called as `Priced.cheapest`.
`Book` implements two interfaces. A class could never extend two classes this way.
`Ebook` overrides the default to apply its own rate.
The cart sees only `Priced`; shipping sees only `Shippable`. Each depends on less.

code.title: Interface plus abstract base
code.caption: Clients use the `Report` interface; `AbstractReport` shares state and a fixed skeleton.

walk.text: The interface is tiny, so fakes and new variants are easy to write.
The abstract class holds state and validates it once in its constructor.
`render()` is `final`: subclasses cannot break the layout, only fill the body.
The abstract `body()` step is the only thing a subclass must supply.
`StockReport` adds its own check after calling `super`.
The client loops over `Report` values and never names a concrete class.

pitfalls: Making clients depend on the abstract class; tests then inherit its state and constructor rules.
Two interfaces with the same default method: the class must override it or will not compile.
Putting mutable shared state in an interface constant; interface fields are always static and final.

quiz.q: Three payment gateways share retry code. Tests need a simple fake. What do clients depend on?
options: An abstract Gateway class holding the retry code
A Gateway interface; real gateways extend an abstract base
A concrete class that tests subclass and override
An interface, with retry code copied into each gateway
quiz.why: Clients need only the role, so the fake implements the interface freely. The abstract base removes duplicated retry code without forcing it on the fake.

takeaway: Interfaces define roles; abstract classes share code behind them.

starters: When should a default method go in an interface instead of a base class?
